D-04  THE RETRIEVAL GATE: `Recall@60 >= 0.80` is currently unreachable.
      What replaces it?
      Affects: T-212, T-213, `configs/default.yaml`, the evaluation chapter
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the decision TASKLIST names explicitly as "a decision for the human,
not a number to chase."

MEASURED 2026-08-26, after two harness defects were found and fixed:

    run                        pool    union recall   Recall@60 (the gate)
    2026-08-25, unranked        447        0.371              0.029
    max_per_source=25, ranked   493        0.371              0.057
    max_per_source=100, ranked 1937        0.714              0.029

Read the middle column first. Union recall is the fraction of your 35 gold
papers that appear ANYWHERE in the retrieved pool. It is a hard ceiling: no
reranker, however good, can put a paper in the top 60 that was never fetched.

    At max_per_source=25 that ceiling is 0.371.
    At max_per_source=100 it is 0.714.
    The gate is 0.80.

So the gate cannot be met at either setting even with a theoretically perfect
ranker. This is not a tuning problem. There are two independent hurdles:
first the union ceiling must exceed 0.80, and only then must 28 of 35 gold
papers be ranked into 60 slots.

WHY, diagnosed three ways:
  - Of the 10 gold papers never retrieved at mps=100, 10/10 are present in
    OpenAlex, 0 are excluded by the year_min=2019 window, and 9/10 are
    findable by exactly the short-query shape already in use. They were not
    unreachable. They were never asked for.
  - Gold papers that ARE pooled rank 38 times across the 15 sub-question
    rankings, but only 2 reach rank <= 4 - and rank <= 4 is all that 60 papers
    split over 15 sub-questions can take.
  - The stock reranker is above chance but only just: 2 top-4 hits against
    1.19 expected at random. Where a query was specific ("scientific survey
    generation") gold landed at ranks 1 and 2. It is under-informed by generic
    queries, not broken.

The 15 queries used are hand-written stand-ins. Generating good ones is the
Planner's job (T-402), which does not exist yet.

OPTIONS
  (a) Keep the gate, re-run after T-402, accept that it may fail.
      Honest, and the re-run is nearly free now (pool caching was added, so it
      costs a re-rank rather than another 18 minutes of S2 backoff). Risk:
      you find out on ~Aug 31 that it still fails, with no time to react.

  (b) Restate the gate to match the geometry.  [RECOMMENDED]
      Report BOTH numbers and gate on the one that measures retrieval rather
      than corpus-size arithmetic:
        - primary gate: union recall over the retrieved pool >= 0.80
          (this measures "did we find it")
        - secondary, reported not gated: Recall@max_papers
          (this measures "did we keep it", and is bounded by max_papers/35)
      This is defensible in the report because it is exactly what the
      measurement showed, and stating it is stronger than quietly missing a
      number you set before you had data.

  (c) Raise `max_papers` from 60 to ~120 so the top-N has room.
      60 papers over ~15 sub-questions is 4 slots each. Doubling gives 8.
      Cost: every downstream stage doubles - the Extractor is 26.6s/paper, so
      120 papers is ~53 minutes of extraction alone, against section 0.2's
      stated ~30-minute tolerance. It also doubles free-tier request
      consumption, which is a hard quota, not a speed setting.

  (d) Bet entirely on T-402 emitting far more specific queries.
      The diagnose_misses evidence says this is plausible - 9/10 misses were
      findable by a short query. But it is a bet on unwritten code, and it has
      to lift union recall from 0.371 to above 0.80.

  (e) Some combination of (b) and a modest max_papers rise (60 -> 80).

RECOMMENDATION: (b) now, and re-run T-212 immediately after T-402 lands. Decide
(c) only with the T-402 numbers in hand.

ANSWER:


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-05  `max_per_source`: stay at 25, or raise to 100?
      Affects: `configs/default.yaml`, run time, D-04
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Currently 25, deliberately unchanged. Raising it to 100 nearly doubles the
union recall ceiling (0.371 -> 0.714) but makes the corpus the Extractor
actually sees WORSE: gold papers in the top 60 fell from 2 to 1. More
candidates genuinely make the top-60 selection harder for a reranker that is
barely above chance on generic queries.

OPTIONS
  (a) Stay at 25 until T-402 exists, then re-measure.  [RECOMMENDED]
      This is what TASKLIST currently says and what the config currently does.
  (b) Raise to 100 now.
      Only sensible if you also take D-04 option (b), where union recall
      becomes the gate - under that framing 100 nearly doubles your headline
      number. Be aware it currently degrades the thing the Extractor reads.
  (c) Split the difference at 50 and measure.
      Costs one eval run (~18 min, or a re-rank if cached). Reasonable if you
      want the curve rather than two points.

ANSWER:


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-06  The Aug 28 kill switch contradicts the Aug 26 measurement. Which wins?
      Affects: T-213, TASKLIST section 13
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
TASKLIST section 13 says: "Aug 28 | Recall@20 < 0.80 | Escalate bge-small ->
bge-base. Spend all of Aug 29 on retrieval. Push M1 to Sep 1."

That row is stale in two ways. It names Recall@20, a metric already retired as
mathematically impossible against a 35-paper gold set (20/35 = 0.57 ceiling).
And it prescribes exactly the escalation the Aug 26 measurement says NOT to
make: ranking is weak because the queries are generic, not because the encoder
is small. Swapping the embedding model would mask that, at a cost of ~6 minutes
per ingestion and a day of schedule.

Tomorrow is Aug 28. If nobody decides this, someone will read that row and
spend Aug 29 on an escalation the evidence has already ruled out.

OPTIONS
  (a) Retire the row. Do not escalate to bge-base. Spend nothing.  [RECOMMENDED]
      Replace it with: "Aug 28 | union recall < 0.40 at mps=25 | re-examine
      the source set, not the encoder."
  (b) Honour the row as written and spend Aug 29 on bge-base.
      Not supported by any measurement you currently hold.

ANSWER:


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-07  T-323: how do you pair a sentence that cites three papers?
      Affects: T-322, T-325, and what the cross-check actually measures
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Only arises if you keep Phase 3B (see D-01). TASKLIST flags it directly: "a
claim sentence citing three papers is not cleanly attributable to one - decide
the rule and write it down, because it changes what the cross-check measures."

OPTIONS
  (a) Drop multi-cite sentences entirely.  [RECOMMENDED]
      Cleanest semantics: every surviving pair is one claim, one source, which
      is exactly what your verifier is trained to judge. Cost: you lose a
      chunk of the data, and survey prose cites multiply quite often, so
      expect to lose a lot. Report the drop rate - it is a limitation, not a
      flaw.
  (b) Pair the sentence against the union of all cited abstracts.
      Keeps the data, but now you are measuring "is this claim supported by
      SOME of this evidence set", which is a different and easier task than
      the one the verifier does in the pipeline. If you choose this, say so
      plainly in the report; a reviewer who notices it unprompted will not be
      generous.
  (c) Pair against each cited abstract separately and score as supported if
      any one supports it.
      Most faithful to how a human wrote the sentence, but it multiplies the
      pair count and biases toward SUPPORT.

Whichever you pick, it goes in the report's method section verbatim.

ANSWER:

================================================================================

D-08  T-707: what target numbers does the report claim?
      Affects: the whole evaluation chapter - and your credibility
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
PROJECT_PLAN section 9 targets groundedness >= 0.9. Nothing peer-reviewed
reaches that on realistic scientific verification: Sarol et al. 0.59 micro-F1,
CliVER 0.797 against clinicians, SurveyGen 35.84% citation accuracy,
SciReviewGen ~30% of chapters at human quality.

TASKLIST is blunt about this: "If the verifier reports 0.9+ against real
citations, suspect the measurement, not a breakthrough."

The decision must be taken BEFORE you see your own numbers. Revising a target
after seeing the result is post-hoc, and an examiner can tell.

OPTIONS
  (a) Revise the target down to an evidence-anchored band now, citing the four
      papers above as the basis.  [RECOMMENDED]
      e.g. groundedness 0.60-0.75 against real citations, with the reasoning
      recorded. Then whatever you measure is interpretable against a stated
      prior.
  (b) Keep 0.9 and report the shortfall honestly.
      Defensible, but you spend the discussion explaining a number you chose
      badly rather than a system you built well.
  (c) Report without any target.
      Weakest option. A measurement with no prior is hard to grade.

ANSWER:


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-09  T-307: when do you escalate deberta-v3-small -> deberta-v3-base?
      Affects: verifier quality, Kaggle quota
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Set the trigger before you see the number, for the same reason as D-08.
Section 0.2 says latency is no longer a constraint and to "lean toward
escalating rather than defending small". Both models train in well under an
hour, so the only real cost is Kaggle quota - which you may also want for

OPTIONS
  (a) Pre-commit a threshold, e.g. "escalate if macro-F1 on the held-out
      SciFact validation split is below 0.75".  [RECOMMENDED]
      Write the number here, before T-303 runs.
  (b) Escalate unconditionally - train both, report both.
      Nearly free on time, and gives you a model-size row in the results
      table. Competes with T-332 for quota if you kept Phase 3C.
  (c) Stay on `small` regardless.
      Only if quota is genuinely tight.

ANSWER (threshold, if (a)):


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-10  T-404: the winning model fills only 4.6 of 8 fields. How much do you
      spend fixing that, and does qwen get a second look?
      Affects: extraction quality, which is a main contribution
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Bake-off result (T-004, measured on 5 real gold abstracts per arm):

    arm                    parse  valid  fields  echo   verdict
    openai/gpt-oss-120b    100%   100%   4.6/8    0     PRIMARY
    qwen/qwen3.6-27b       100%   100%   7.0/8    2/5   rejected

qwen fills more fields but echoed the literal schema placeholder "string" into
`datasets`/`metrics` on 2 of 5 papers. That parses, validates, and silently
injects fabricated content into a hallucination-graded pipeline - exactly what
SPEC section 14.2 forbids. Excluding those rows it scores 6.33/8, not 7.0.

The suspicion recorded in TASKLIST is that 4.6/8 is a PROMPT problem, not a
model problem: `extractor_v1.md` ships 3 few-shot examples against the ~20 that

OPTIONS

      If better examples eliminate the placeholder echo, qwen's coverage
      advantage becomes real. Risk: the echo is a model habit, not a prompting
      artefact, and you will have spent the time to find out. Only do this if
      (a) leaves you short.
  (c) Accept 4.6/8 and move on.
      Only if you are behind on M1. Half your schema being empty is a visible
      weakness in the insight table the examiner will look at.

ANSWER:


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
D-11  T-610: how is the system demonstrated at the viva?
      TASKLIST: "Decide this now, not the night before."
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A 60-paper run is 20-40 minutes on CPU against a rate-limited free tier. That
cannot be run live in front of an examiner.

OPTIONS

Written to `decisions.txt` — 16 decisions with an `ANSWER:` slot under each, organised by when they have to be taken.

**Decide today (3)**

- **D-01 — Scope.** The big one. TASKLIST adds three tracks explicitly off the critical path: Phase 3B (SciReviewGen), 3C (reranker fine-tune), 6B (Postgres). That's 21 of ~85 open tasks — a quarter of everything left — and none is needed for the pipeline to run. They're not equally droppable: 3B contains T-325, which is on the never-cut list and is your only answer to the circularity trap; 3C is a weight swap with an adoption gate that may reject it anyway; 6B is seven tasks to make three slides true. Recommended: keep 3B, drop 3C and 6B, fix the slides instead.
- **D-02 — Start Kaggle training.** Phase 3 was supposed to start "the moment T-001/T-002 close." They closed Aug 25; it's Aug 27 and nothing is on disk. The Aug 29 kill switch costs you T-305, the table that justifies the training component.
- **D-03 — The S2 key.**

**Decide by Aug 29 (4)** — D-04 is the one TASKLIST flags as yours, and the framing matters: **union recall is a hard ceiling on Recall@60.** At `mps=25` it's 0.371, at `mps=100` it's 0.714, and the gate is 0.80. So the gate is unreachable at either setting *even with a theoretically perfect reranker* — it's not a tuning problem. Five options laid out, recommending you gate on union recall and report Recall@max_papers alongside.

**Two things I found while reading that aren't in TASKLIST as decisions:**

**D-06 — the Aug 28 kill switch contradicts the Aug 26 measurement.** §13 says "Recall@20 < 0.80 → escalate `bge-small` → `bge-base`, spend all of Aug 29 on retrieval." [build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "researchgpt"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A Multi-Agent Agentic RAG Platform for Automated Literature Review"
readme = "README.md"
requires-python = ">=3.11"
license = { text = "MIT" }
authors = [
    { name = "Abrarullah Mohammed" },
    { name = "G. Shashivadan Rao" },
    { name = "P. Sreekaran Reddy" },
]

# Runtime deps are grouped so a partial install still gets you a working CLI.
# Verified to resolve on Python 3.14.6 (2026-08-25).
dependencies = [
    "pydantic>=2.7",
    "pyyaml>=6.0",
    "typer>=0.12",
    "httpx>=0.27",
    "python-dotenv>=1.0",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
# Phase 2 — retrieval. Heavy (pulls torch); install when Phase 2 starts.
retrieval = [
    "chromadb>=1.0",
    "rank-bm25>=0.2.2",
    "sentence-transformers>=3.0",
    "pymupdf>=1.24",
]
# Phase 4/5 — the agent graph.
graph = [
    "langgraph>=0.2",
    "langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite>=1.0",
]
# Phase 5 — verifier inference on CPU. No torch needed at run time.
verify = [
    "onnxruntime>=1.18",
    "transformers>=4.40",
    # DeBERTa-v3 uses a SentencePiece tokenizer. Without these two the
    # tokenizer fails to load with a misleading "conversion" error - verified
    # missing on this machine 2026-08-25. Kaggle ships them; local does not.
    "sentencepiece>=0.2",
    "protobuf>=4.25",
    "optimum[onnxruntime]>=1.20",   # ONNX export + int8 quantization (T-304)
]
# Phase 6 — API layer.
api = [
    "fastapi>=0.110",
    "uvicorn[standard]>=0.29",
    "sse-starlette>=2.0",
]
# Phase 3B — SciReviewGen parsing.
scireviewgen = [
    "datasets>=2.19",
    "pyarrow>=16.0",
]
dev = [
    "pytest>=8.0",
    "pytest-asyncio>=0.23",
    "ruff>=0.4",
]

[project.scripts]
researchgpt = "researchgpt.cli:app"

[tool.hatch.build.targets.wheel]
packages = ["src/researchgpt"]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
target-version = "py311"

[tool.ruff.lint]
select = ["E", "F", "I", "UP", "B"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
testpaths = ["tests"]
pythonpath = ["src"]

"""The three-way verdict vocabulary, in one place.

Everything downstream keys off this ordering: the training notebook's
classification head, the ONNX export, the softmax column indices in
``agents/verifier.py`` and the T-305 report all assume ``LABELS`` order.
Changing it silently invalidates a trained checkpoint, so it is isolated here
rather than being re-declared per module.

⚠️ SciFact spells the third class ``NEI``, not ``NOT_ENOUGH_INFO``. The SPEC §8
``Verdict`` vocabulary is a different, wider thing (it has ``PARTIAL``, which no
classifier predicts — T-503 derives it from ``support_score``). Do not conflate
the two: this is the *model's* label set, not the pipeline's verdict set.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

#: Canonical order. The trained head's logit columns follow this exactly.
LABELS: tuple[str, ...] = ("SUPPORT", "CONTRADICT", "NEI")

LABEL2ID: dict[str, int] = {label: i for i, label in enumerate(LABELS)}
ID2LABEL: dict[int, str] = {i: label for i, label in enumerate(LABELS)}

#: Maps the *stock* ``cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-*`` head onto ours, for the
#: T-305 stock-vs-fine-tuned comparison. Those checkpoints are trained on
#: SNLI/MNLI and emit lowercase NLI names in a different order, so a naive
#: argmax comparison would score the stock model at near chance for the wrong
#: reason. Verified against the checkpoint's own ``config.id2label`` at load
#: time by ``evaluate.py`` — this table is the expectation, not a guess.
NLI_TO_VERDICT: dict[str, str] = {
    "entailment": "SUPPORT",
    "contradiction": "CONTRADICT",
    "neutral": "NEI",
}

__all__ = ["LABELS", "LABEL2ID", "ID2LABEL", "NLI_TO_VERDICT"]

"""T-301 — build ``(claim, evidence_sentence) -> SUPPORT | CONTRADICT | NEI`` pairs.

Source: ``allenai/scifact_entailment`` (919 train / 340 validation rows).

⚠️ **Two loading facts, both found the hard way.**

1. TASKLIST T-301 says to use ``scifact_entailment`` because plain
   ``allenai/scifact`` is script-based and returns HTTP 501. **That is only half
   right — verified 2026-08-27: ``scifact_entailment`` is *also* script-based**,
   and ``datasets>=4`` refuses it outright with
   ``RuntimeError: Dataset scripts are no longer supported``. The 2026-08-25
   pre-check passed because it probed the datasets-server API, not
   ``load_dataset``.
2. The fix is the Hub's **auto-converted parquet branch**,
   ``refs/convert/parquet``, which carries the identical rows with no script.
   That is what :func:`load_split` reads. It needs no token for this dataset and
   works the same on Kaggle.

**Row shape** (verified 2026-08-27, not copied from the card)::

    claim_id     int         # repeats: one claim pairs with up to 5 abstracts
    claim        str
    abstract_id  int
    title        str
    abstract     list[str]   # the abstract already split into sentences
    verdict      str         # SUPPORT | CONTRADICT | NEI
    evidence     list[int]   # sentence indices into `abstract`; [] iff NEI

Checked over all 1,259 rows: zero out-of-range evidence indices, zero NEI rows
carrying evidence, abstracts run 3–25 sentences.

**Pairing rule** (TASKLIST T-301):

* ``SUPPORT`` / ``CONTRADICT`` — pair the claim with *each* sentence named in
  ``evidence``. A 3-sentence evidence set becomes 3 training pairs.
* ``NEI`` — ``evidence`` is empty, so sample ``nei_per_claim`` sentences from
  that row's abstract. The abstract is a genuine retrieved-but-non-supporting
  abstract for that claim, so its sentences really are "not enough info".

Deliberately **not** done: mining extra NEI pairs from the *non*-evidence
sentences of SUPPORT/CONTRADICT abstracts. Those sentences sit in an abstract
that does support the claim, so a near-paraphrase of the evidence would be
labelled NEI and teach the model the opposite of its job. The cheap volume is
not worth the label noise.

⚠️ **The internal split groups by ``claim_id``.** One claim appears in up to 5
rows, so a row-level split puts the same claim on both sides and inflates the
dev score — the identical failure mode TASKLIST flags for T-330. The reported
held-out set (T-305) is the untouched ``validation`` split; ``dev`` exists only
for tuning.

Run::

    python -m researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs
    python -m researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs --nei-per-claim 3 --out data/scifact
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import random
from collections import Counter
from typing import Any

from researchgpt.verify.labels import LABELS

#: The dataset repo and the parquet branch the loader actually reads.
_REPO = "allenai/scifact_entailment"
_REVISION = "refs/convert/parquet"
_PARQUET = "default/{split}/0000.parquet"

#: Row counts published on the dataset card. :func:`load_split` checks against
#: these and warns on a mismatch — a silently re-converted parquet branch would

"""T-305 — stock vs fine-tuned verifier, on the same untouched held-out set.

This is the headline result that justifies the training component, and a graded
deliverable in its own right (TASKLIST T-305). It also implements the **T-307
escalation gate**: macro-F1 below :data:`ESCALATION_THRESHOLD` on the held-out
set means retrain at ``deberta-v3-base``.

Two details here are load-bearing and easy to get silently wrong.

**1. Pair order is (evidence, claim), not (claim, evidence).**
The cross-encoder is an NLI model: input is ``(premise, hypothesis)``. The
evidence sentence is the premise and the claim is the hypothesis being tested
against it. Reversing them trains and scores a subtly different task and costs
several F1 points for no visible reason. :func:`encode_pair` is the single
place this order is decided; the training notebook imports the same convention.

**2. The stock head is in a different order from ours.**
``cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-*`` emits ``{0: contradiction, 1: entailment,
2: neutral}``; :data:`~researchgpt.verify.labels.LABELS` is ``(SUPPORT,
CONTRADICT, NEI)``. A naive argmax comparison scores the stock model near
chance *for the wrong reason* and would make the fine-tune look far better than
it is. :func:`label_permutation` derives the mapping from the checkpoint's own
``config.id2label`` at load time and raises if it cannot — it never guesses.

Run::

    # stock zero-shot baseline only
    python -m researchgpt.verify.evaluate --stock cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small

    # the full T-305 table, once Kaggle returns the checkpoint
    python -m researchgpt.verify.evaluate \\
        --stock cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small \\
        --tuned data/models/verifier-scifact
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
from typing import Any

from researchgpt.verify.labels import ID2LABEL, LABEL2ID, LABELS, NLI_TO_VERDICT
from researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs import read_jsonl

#: T-307 escalation gate. Decided in `decisions.txt` D-09 (2026-08-27):
#: "escalate if macro-F1 on the held-out SciFact validation split is below 0.75".
#: Fixed *before* the first training run, so the decision is not post-hoc.
ESCALATION_THRESHOLD = 0.75

#: The verified escalation target. Same tokenizer family, ~184M vs ~44M.
ESCALATION_MODEL = "cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base"

DEFAULT_PAIRS = pathlib.Path("data/scifact/pairs_validation.jsonl")


def encode_pair(pair: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """The one place the (premise, hypothesis) order is decided.

    Premise = the evidence sentence. Hypothesis = the claim under test.
    Training and inference must both call this; do not inline the tuple.
    """
    return pair["evidence"], pair["claim"]


def label_permutation(id2label: dict[int, str]) -> list[int]:
    """Column indices that reorder a checkpoint's logits into ``LABELS`` order.

    ``logits[:, permutation]`` puts SUPPORT first, CONTRADICT second, NEI third.

    Accepts either a head already trained in our vocabulary (``SUPPORT``/...)
    or a stock NLI head (``entailment``/``contradiction``/``neutral``). Raises
    on anything else rather than guessing — a wrong permutation is invisible in
    the output and poisons every number downstream.
    """
    normalised: dict[str, int] = {}
    for idx, raw in id2label.items():
        name = str(raw).strip()
        verdict = name.upper() if name.upper() in LABEL2ID else NLI_TO_VERDICT.get(name.lower())
        if verdict is None:
            raise ValueError(
                f"Cannot map checkpoint label {raw!r} onto {LABELS}. "
                f"Checkpoint id2label={id2label}. Refusing to guess a permutation."
            )
        normalised[verdict] = int(idx)

"""Source-of-truth cells for the T-302 Kaggle notebook.

Kept as a plain .py so the training logic can be smoke-tested locally on CPU
before it is packed into the .ipynb. Cell boundaries are `# %% [markdown]` and
`# %% [code]`; build_ipynb.py splits on those.
"""

CELLS = []


def md(text):
    CELLS.append(("markdown", text.strip("\n")))


def code(text):
    CELLS.append(("code", text.strip("\n")))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 0. title
md(r"""
# T-302 / T-303 — Verifier fine-tune (SciFact → DeBERTa-v3)

**ResearchGPT**, Phase 3. This notebook trains **the graded component**: the
three-way claim verifier that decides whether a drafted claim is `SUPPORT`,
`CONTRADICT` or `NEI` against a retrieved evidence sentence.

| | |
|---|---|
| Task | T-302 (author) / T-303 (run) |
| Base | `cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small` (~44M, ungated, safetensors) |
| Data | `allenai/scifact_entailment`, paired per TASKLIST T-301 |
| Runtime | **GPU T4 x2** (single GPU is used; ~10–20 min) |
| Internet | **must be ON** (Settings → Internet) |
| Output | `verifier-scifact/` checkpoint + `verifier_metrics.json` |

### What it produces
1. A fine-tuned checkpoint, ready for the T-304 ONNX int8 export.
2. **The T-305 table** — stock vs fine-tuned on the *same* untouched held-out
   set, which is the headline result justifying the training component.
3. **The T-307 verdict** — escalate to `deberta-v3-base` or not, against the
   0.75 macro-F1 threshold fixed in `decisions.txt` D-09 *before* this ran.

### Two things that are easy to get wrong, and are handled here
* **Pair order is `(evidence, claim)`** — premise then hypothesis. This is an
  NLI model; reversing them silently trains a different task.
* **The stock head is `{0: contradiction, 1: entailment, 2: neutral}`**, which
  is *not* our label order. The head is **permuted, not reinitialised**, so the
  fine-tune starts from a model that already knows entailment. The same
  permutation is what lets the stock arm be scored fairly in T-305.
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 1. config
md(r"""
## 1 · Configuration

`BASE_MODEL` is the only line to change for the **T-307 escalation**: swap in
`cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base` and re-run the whole notebook top to bottom.
Everything else is deliberately fixed — `SEED` in particular, because the T-301
pairing is a pure function of it and the local `data/scifact/*.jsonl` must match
what trains here.
""")

code(r"""
# --- T-307 escalation: change ONLY this line and re-run -----------------
BASE_MODEL = "cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small"     # ~44M
# BASE_MODEL = "cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base"    # ~184M, escalation target
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

SEED            = 20260827   # must equal researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs.SEED
NEI_PER_CLAIM   = 2          # must equal the local build
DEV_FRAC        = 0.15
EPOCHS          = 3          # TASKLIST T-302: 2-3
LEARNING_RATE   = 2e-5
BATCH_SIZE      = 32
MAX_LENGTH      = 256
OUTPUT_DIR      = "/kaggle/working/verifier-scifact"

ESCALATION_THRESHOLD = 0.75  # decisions.txt D-09, fixed before this ran
LABELS = ("SUPPORT", "CONTRADICT", "NEI")
LABEL2ID = {l: i for i, l in enumerate(LABELS)}
ID2LABEL = {i: l for i, l in enumerate(LABELS)}

print("base model :", BASE_MODEL)
print("labels     :", LABELS)
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 2. deps
md(r"""
## 2 · Dependencies

Kaggle's images ship `transformers`, `torch`, `sentencepiece` and `protobuf`
already — the last two matter because **DeBERTa-v3 uses a SentencePiece
tokenizer** and fails with a misleading "conversion" error without them
(TASKLIST T-306 records them missing on the local machine; Kaggle has them).

The cell is tolerant: it installs only what is actually absent, so a re-run
costs seconds rather than re-resolving the whole environment.
""")

code(r"""
import importlib, subprocess, sys

def ensure(pkg, import_name=None):
    try:
        importlib.import_module(import_name or pkg.split("==")[0].replace("-", "_"))
        print(f"  present : {pkg}")
    except ImportError:
        print(f"  install : {pkg}")
        subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pkg])

for pkg, mod in [("transformers", "transformers"),
                 ("sentencepiece", "sentencepiece"),
                 ("protobuf", "google.protobuf"),
                 ("pyarrow", "pyarrow"),
                 ("huggingface_hub", "huggingface_hub"),
                 ("scikit-learn", "sklearn")]:
    ensure(pkg, mod)

import torch, transformers
print("\ntorch        :", torch.__version__)
print("transformers :", transformers.__version__)
print("cuda         :", torch.cuda.is_available(),
      torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 3. data
md(r"""
## 3 · Build the T-301 pairs

⚠️ **`allenai/scifact_entailment` cannot be loaded with `load_dataset`.** It is a
*script-based* dataset and `datasets>=4` refuses it outright
(`RuntimeError: Dataset scripts are no longer supported`). TASKLIST T-301 says
this is true of plain `allenai/scifact` only — verified 2026-08-27, it is true
of `scifact_entailment` as well.

The fix is the Hub's auto-converted **parquet branch**, `refs/convert/parquet`,
which carries identical rows with no script and needs no token.

> **This cell is a mirror of `src/researchgpt/verify/scifact_pairs.py`.** Keep
> the two in sync — `tests/test_phase3_acceptance.py` asserts that this notebook
> and the module produce byte-identical pairs, and fails if they drift.
""")

code(r"""
import json, random
from collections import Counter
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

_REPO, _REVISION = "allenai/scifact_entailment", "refs/convert/parquet"
EXPECTED_ROWS = {"train": 919, "validation": 340}

def load_split(split):
    path = hf_hub_download(_REPO, f"default/{split}/0000.parquet",
                           repo_type="dataset", revision=_REVISION)
    rows = pq.read_table(path).to_pylist()
    exp = EXPECTED_ROWS.get(split)
    if exp is not None and len(rows) != exp:
        print(f"  WARNING: {split}: got {len(rows)} rows, expected {exp}.")
    return rows

def build_pairs(rows, *, nei_per_claim=2, seed=SEED):
    """SUPPORT/CONTRADICT -> one pair per annotated evidence sentence.
    NEI -> sample `nei_per_claim` sentences from that row's abstract."""
    rng, pairs = random.Random(seed), []
    for row in rows:
        verdict = row["verdict"]
        sentences = list(row["abstract"])
        if not sentences:
            continue
        if verdict == "NEI":
            k = min(nei_per_claim, len(sentences))
            indices = sorted(rng.sample(range(len(sentences)), k))
        else:
            indices = [i for i in row["evidence"] if 0 <= i < len(sentences)]
            if not indices:
                continue
        for i in indices:
            pairs.append({"claim": row["claim"], "evidence": sentences[i],
                          "label": verdict, "claim_id": row["claim_id"],
                          "abstract_id": row["abstract_id"], "sentence_index": i})
    return pairs

def split_by_claim(pairs, *, dev_frac=DEV_FRAC, seed=SEED):
    """Group by claim_id. A row-level split leaks: one claim spans up to 5
    abstracts, so the same claim text would sit on both sides."""
    claim_ids = sorted({p["claim_id"] for p in pairs})
    rng = random.Random(seed); rng.shuffle(claim_ids)
    dev_ids = set(claim_ids[:int(round(len(claim_ids) * dev_frac))])
    return ([p for p in pairs if p["claim_id"] not in dev_ids],
            [p for p in pairs if p["claim_id"] in dev_ids])

raw_train, raw_val = load_split("train"), load_split("validation")
all_train = build_pairs(raw_train, nei_per_claim=NEI_PER_CLAIM)
val_pairs = build_pairs(raw_val,  nei_per_claim=NEI_PER_CLAIM)
train_pairs, dev_pairs = split_by_claim(all_train)

assert not ({p["claim_id"] for p in train_pairs} & {p["claim_id"] for p in dev_pairs}), \
    "claim_id leaked across the train/dev split"

for name, ps in [("train", train_pairs), ("dev", dev_pairs), ("validation", val_pairs)]:
    c = Counter(p["label"] for p in ps)
    print(f"  {name:12s} pairs {len(ps):5d}  claims {len({p['claim_id'] for p in ps}):4d}  "
          + "  ".join(f"{k} {c.get(k,0):4d}" for k in LABELS))

print("\n  OK: no claim_id appears in both train and dev")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 4. tokenize
md(r"""
## 4 · Tokenize

**Premise = evidence, hypothesis = claim.** One helper, used by training and by
every evaluation below, so the order cannot drift between them.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
print("tokenizer:", type(tokenizer).__name__)

def encode_pair(pair):
    """(premise, hypothesis) = (evidence sentence, claim under test)."""
    return pair["evidence"], pair["claim"]

class PairDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, pairs, tokenizer, max_length=MAX_LENGTH):
        premises   = [encode_pair(p)[0] for p in pairs]
        hypotheses = [encode_pair(p)[1] for p in pairs]
        self.enc = tokenizer(premises, hypotheses, truncation=True,
                             max_length=max_length, padding=False)
        self.labels = [LABEL2ID[p["label"]] for p in pairs]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.labels)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        item = {k: v[i] for k, v in self.enc.items()}
        item["labels"] = self.labels[i]
        return item

train_ds = PairDataset(train_pairs, tokenizer)
dev_ds   = PairDataset(dev_pairs,   tokenizer)
val_ds   = PairDataset(val_pairs,   tokenizer)

lens = [len(x) for x in train_ds.enc["input_ids"]]
print(f"train {len(train_ds)}  dev {len(dev_ds)}  validation {len(val_ds)}")
print(f"token length: mean {sum(lens)/len(lens):.0f}  max {max(lens)}  "
      f"truncated at {MAX_LENGTH}: {sum(1 for l in lens if l >= MAX_LENGTH)}")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 5. warm start
md(r"""
## 5 · Warm start — permute the head, do not reinitialise it

`cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-*` already has a trained 3-way NLI head, but in
the order `{0: contradiction, 1: entailment, 2: neutral}`. Ours is
`(SUPPORT, CONTRADICT, NEI)` = `(entailment, contradiction, neutral)`.

Loading with `ignore_mismatched_sizes` or a fresh head throws away a head that
already solves 2/3 of this problem. **Permuting rows `[1, 0, 2]` keeps it.**
The permutation is derived from the checkpoint's own `config.id2label` and
asserted, never hard-coded.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoConfig

NLI_TO_VERDICT = {"entailment": "SUPPORT",
                  "contradiction": "CONTRADICT",
                  "neutral": "NEI"}

def label_permutation(id2label):
    """Column indices reordering a checkpoint's logits into LABELS order."""
    normalised = {}
    for idx, raw in id2label.items():
        name = str(raw).strip()
        verdict = name.upper() if name.upper() in LABEL2ID else NLI_TO_VERDICT.get(name.lower())
        if verdict is None:
            raise ValueError(f"cannot map checkpoint label {raw!r} onto {LABELS}")
        normalised[verdict] = int(idx)
    missing = [l for l in LABELS if l not in normalised]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"checkpoint head missing {missing}; id2label={id2label}")
    return [normalised[l] for l in LABELS]

stock_config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
PERM = label_permutation(stock_config.id2label)
print("stock id2label :", stock_config.id2label)
print("permutation    :", PERM, "->", LABELS)

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    BASE_MODEL, num_labels=3, id2label=ID2LABEL, label2id=LABEL2ID)

with torch.no_grad():
    w, b = model.classifier.weight.data, model.classifier.bias.data
    model.classifier.weight.data = w[PERM].clone()
    model.classifier.bias.data   = b[PERM].clone()

print("head permuted into", LABELS, "order")
print("params:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e6, "M")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 6. metrics
md(r"""
## 6 · Metrics

Hand-written rather than pulled from sklearn so the zero-division convention is
explicit: a class the model never predicts scores precision **0**, not NaN. This
mirrors `researchgpt.verify.evaluate.score` exactly.
""")

code(r"""
import numpy as np

def score(y_true, y_pred):
    n = len(LABELS)
    confusion = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
    for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred):
        confusion[int(t)][int(p)] += 1
    per_class, f1s = {}, []
    for i, label in enumerate(LABELS):
        tp = confusion[i][i]
        fp = sum(confusion[j][i] for j in range(n)) - tp
        fn = sum(confusion[i]) - tp
        prec = tp/(tp+fp) if (tp+fp) else 0.0
        rec  = tp/(tp+fn) if (tp+fn) else 0.0
        f1   = 2*prec*rec/(prec+rec) if (prec+rec) else 0.0
        per_class[label] = {"precision": prec, "recall": rec, "f1": f1,
                            "support": sum(confusion[i])}
        f1s.append(f1)
    return {"per_class": per_class, "macro_f1": sum(f1s)/n,
            "accuracy": sum(confusion[i][i] for i in range(n))/max(len(y_true), 1),
            "confusion": confusion, "n": len(y_true)}

def report(name, r):
    print(f"{name}   n={r['n']}  accuracy={r['accuracy']:.3f}  macro-F1={r['macro_f1']:.3f}")
    print(f"  {'class':12s} {'P':>7s} {'R':>7s} {'F1':>7s} {'support':>8s}")
    for label, m in r["per_class"].items():
        print(f"  {label:12s} {m['precision']:7.3f} {m['recall']:7.3f} "
              f"{m['f1']:7.3f} {m['support']:8d}")
    print(f"  confusion (rows=true {list(LABELS)}, cols=pred):")
    for i, row in enumerate(r["confusion"]):
        print(f"    {LABELS[i]:12s} {row}")

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    preds = np.asarray(logits).argmax(-1)
    r = score(list(labels), list(preds))
    out = {"accuracy": r["accuracy"], "macro_f1": r["macro_f1"]}
    for label, m in r["per_class"].items():
        out[f"f1_{label}"] = m["f1"]
    return out
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 7. stock baseline
md(r"""
## 7 · Stock baseline — **before** training

Scored here, on the untouched `validation` split, through the same permutation.
This is the `stock` row of the T-305 table. Taking it now means the comparison
is against the identical data and identical code path as the tuned arm.
""")

code(r"""
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from transformers import DataCollatorWithPadding

collator = DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

@torch.no_grad()
def predict(m, dataset, permutation=None, batch_size=64):
    m.eval().to(device)
    loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=collator)
    preds = []
    for batch in loader:
        batch = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in batch.items()}
        batch.pop("labels", None)
        logits = m(**batch).logits
        if permutation is not None:
            logits = logits[:, permutation]
        preds.extend(logits.argmax(-1).cpu().tolist())
    return preds

stock_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
y_true = [LABEL2ID[p["label"]] for p in val_pairs]
stock_result = score(y_true, predict(stock_model, val_ds, permutation=PERM))
report("stock (zero-shot)", stock_result)

del stock_model
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 8. train
md(r"""
## 8 · Train

Cross-entropy, fixed seed, `macro_f1` on the claim-grouped **dev** split chooses
the best checkpoint. The held-out `validation` split is not looked at until
section 9 — it is the number that gets reported, so it must not steer training.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments, set_seed

set_seed(SEED)

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="/kaggle/working/checkpoints",
    seed=SEED,
    data_seed=SEED,
    num_train_epochs=EPOCHS,
    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
    per_device_train_batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=64,
    warmup_ratio=0.1,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_steps=25,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    save_total_limit=1,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="macro_f1",
    greater_is_better=True,
    fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(),
    report_to=[],
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=train_ds,
    eval_dataset=dev_ds,
    data_collator=collator,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
)

train_result = trainer.train()
print("\ntrain runtime: %.1f s" % train_result.metrics["train_runtime"])
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 9. evaluate
md(r"""
## 9 · T-305 — stock vs fine-tuned on the held-out set

The first time `validation` is used for anything.
""")

code(r"""
tuned_result = score(y_true, predict(trainer.model, val_ds))
report("fine-tuned", tuned_result)

print("\n" + "="*72)
print("T-305 - STOCK vs FINE-TUNED (same held-out set, n=%d)" % tuned_result["n"])
print("="*72)
hdr = f"  {'arm':14s} {'acc':>7s} {'macro-F1':>9s} " + " ".join(f"{l[:9]+' F1':>13s}" for l in LABELS)
print(hdr)
for name, r in (("stock", stock_result), ("fine-tuned", tuned_result)):
    row = f"  {name:14s} {r['accuracy']:7.3f} {r['macro_f1']:9.3f} "
    row += " ".join(f"{r['per_class'][l]['f1']:13.3f}" for l in LABELS)
    print(row)
print(f"  {'delta':14s} {tuned_result['accuracy']-stock_result['accuracy']:+7.3f} "
      f"{tuned_result['macro_f1']-stock_result['macro_f1']:+9.3f}")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 10. gate
md(r"""
## 10 · T-307 escalation gate

Threshold fixed at **0.75 macro-F1** in `decisions.txt` D-09, *before* this run.
It is applied mechanically so the decision cannot be rationalised after seeing
the number.
""")

code(r"""
macro_f1 = tuned_result["macro_f1"]
escalate = macro_f1 < ESCALATION_THRESHOLD

print("="*72)
if escalate:
    print(f"T-307 GATE: ESCALATE.  macro-F1 {macro_f1:.3f} < {ESCALATION_THRESHOLD}")
    print("  -> set BASE_MODEL = 'cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base' in section 1")
    print("     and re-run this notebook top to bottom.")

Kept as a plain .py so the training logic can be smoke-tested locally on CPU
before it is packed into the .ipynb. Cell boundaries are `# %% [markdown]` and
`# %% [code]`; build_ipynb.py splits on those.
"""

CELLS = []


def md(text):
    CELLS.append(("markdown", text.strip("\n")))


def code(text):
    CELLS.append(("code", text.strip("\n")))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 0. title
md(r"""
# T-302 / T-303 — Verifier fine-tune (SciFact → DeBERTa-v3)

**ResearchGPT**, Phase 3. This notebook trains **the graded component**: the
three-way claim verifier that decides whether a drafted claim is `SUPPORT`,
`CONTRADICT` or `NEI` against a retrieved evidence sentence.

| | |
|---|---|
| Task | T-302 (author) / T-303 (run) |
| Base | `cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small` (~44M, ungated, safetensors) |
| Data | `allenai/scifact_entailment`, paired per TASKLIST T-301 |
| Runtime | **GPU T4 x2** (single GPU is used; ~10–20 min) |
| Internet | **must be ON** (Settings → Internet) |
| Output | `verifier-scifact/` checkpoint + `verifier_metrics.json` |

### What it produces
1. A fine-tuned checkpoint, ready for the T-304 ONNX int8 export.
2. **The T-305 table** — stock vs fine-tuned on the *same* untouched held-out
   set, which is the headline result justifying the training component.
3. **The T-307 verdict** — escalate to `deberta-v3-base` or not, against the
   0.75 macro-F1 threshold fixed in `decisions.txt` D-09 *before* this ran.

### Two things that are easy to get wrong, and are handled here
* **Pair order is `(evidence, claim)`** — premise then hypothesis. This is an
  NLI model; reversing them silently trains a different task.
* **The stock head is `{0: contradiction, 1: entailment, 2: neutral}`**, which
  is *not* our label order. The head is **permuted, not reinitialised**, so the
  fine-tune starts from a model that already knows entailment. The same
  permutation is what lets the stock arm be scored fairly in T-305.
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 1. config
md(r"""
## 1 · Configuration

`BASE_MODEL` is the only line to change for the **T-307 escalation**: swap in
`cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base` and re-run the whole notebook top to bottom.
Everything else is deliberately fixed — `SEED` in particular, because the T-301
pairing is a pure function of it and the local `data/scifact/*.jsonl` must match
what trains here.
""")

# --- T-307 escalation: change ONLY this line and re-run -----------------
BASE_MODEL = "cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small"     # ~44M
# BASE_MODEL = "cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base"    # ~184M, escalation target
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------

NEI_PER_CLAIM   = 2          # must equal the local build
DEV_FRAC        = 0.15
EPOCHS          = 3          # TASKLIST T-302: 2-3
LEARNING_RATE   = 2e-5
BATCH_SIZE      = 32
MAX_LENGTH      = 256
OUTPUT_DIR      = "/kaggle/working/verifier-scifact"

ESCALATION_THRESHOLD = 0.75  # decisions.txt D-09, fixed before this ran

""")

md(r"""
## 2 · Dependencies

Kaggle's images ship `transformers`, `torch`, `sentencepiece` and `protobuf`
already — the last two matter because **DeBERTa-v3 uses a SentencePiece
tokenizer** and fails with a misleading "conversion" error without them
(TASKLIST T-306 records them missing on the local machine; Kaggle has them).

The cell is tolerant: it installs only what is actually absent, so a re-run
costs seconds rather than re-resolving the whole environment.
""")

code(r"""
import importlib, subprocess, sys

def ensure(pkg, import_name=None):
    try:
        importlib.import_module(import_name or pkg.split("==")[0].replace("-", "_"))
        print(f"  present : {pkg}")
    except ImportError:
        print(f"  install : {pkg}")
        subprocess.check_call([sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install", "-q", pkg])

for pkg, mod in [("transformers", "transformers"),
                 ("sentencepiece", "sentencepiece"),
                 ("protobuf", "google.protobuf"),
                 ("pyarrow", "pyarrow"),
                 ("huggingface_hub", "huggingface_hub"),
                 ("scikit-learn", "sklearn")]:
    ensure(pkg, mod)

import torch, transformers
print("\ntorch        :", torch.__version__)
print("transformers :", transformers.__version__)
print("cuda         :", torch.cuda.is_available(),
      torch.cuda.get_device_name(0) if torch.cuda.is_available() else "")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 3. data
md(r"""
## 3 · Build the T-301 pairs

⚠️ **`allenai/scifact_entailment` cannot be loaded with `load_dataset`.** It is a
*script-based* dataset and `datasets>=4` refuses it outright
(`RuntimeError: Dataset scripts are no longer supported`). TASKLIST T-301 says
this is true of plain `allenai/scifact` only — verified 2026-08-27, it is true
of `scifact_entailment` as well.

The fix is the Hub's auto-converted **parquet branch**, `refs/convert/parquet`,
which carries identical rows with no script and needs no token.

> **This cell is a mirror of `src/researchgpt/verify/scifact_pairs.py`.** Keep
> the two in sync — `tests/test_phase3_acceptance.py` asserts that this notebook
> and the module produce byte-identical pairs, and fails if they drift.
""")

code(r"""
import json, random
from collections import Counter
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import pyarrow.parquet as pq

_REPO, _REVISION = "allenai/scifact_entailment", "refs/convert/parquet"
EXPECTED_ROWS = {"train": 919, "validation": 340}

def load_split(split):
    path = hf_hub_download(_REPO, f"default/{split}/0000.parquet",
                           repo_type="dataset", revision=_REVISION)
    rows = pq.read_table(path).to_pylist()
    exp = EXPECTED_ROWS.get(split)
    if exp is not None and len(rows) != exp:
        print(f"  WARNING: {split}: got {len(rows)} rows, expected {exp}.")
    return rows

def build_pairs(rows, *, nei_per_claim=2, seed=SEED):
    """SUPPORT/CONTRADICT -> one pair per annotated evidence sentence.
    NEI -> sample `nei_per_claim` sentences from that row's abstract."""
    rng, pairs = random.Random(seed), []
    for row in rows:
        verdict = row["verdict"]
        sentences = list(row["abstract"])
        if not sentences:
            continue
        if verdict == "NEI":
            k = min(nei_per_claim, len(sentences))
            indices = sorted(rng.sample(range(len(sentences)), k))
        else:
            indices = [i for i in row["evidence"] if 0 <= i < len(sentences)]
            if not indices:
                continue
        for i in indices:
            pairs.append({"claim": row["claim"], "evidence": sentences[i],
                          "label": verdict, "claim_id": row["claim_id"],
                          "abstract_id": row["abstract_id"], "sentence_index": i})
    return pairs

def split_by_claim(pairs, *, dev_frac=DEV_FRAC, seed=SEED):
    """Group by claim_id. A row-level split leaks: one claim spans up to 5
    abstracts, so the same claim text would sit on both sides."""
    claim_ids = sorted({p["claim_id"] for p in pairs})
    rng = random.Random(seed); rng.shuffle(claim_ids)
    dev_ids = set(claim_ids[:int(round(len(claim_ids) * dev_frac))])
    return ([p for p in pairs if p["claim_id"] not in dev_ids],
            [p for p in pairs if p["claim_id"] in dev_ids])

raw_train, raw_val = load_split("train"), load_split("validation")
all_train = build_pairs(raw_train, nei_per_claim=NEI_PER_CLAIM)
val_pairs = build_pairs(raw_val,  nei_per_claim=NEI_PER_CLAIM)
train_pairs, dev_pairs = split_by_claim(all_train)

assert not ({p["claim_id"] for p in train_pairs} & {p["claim_id"] for p in dev_pairs}), \
    "claim_id leaked across the train/dev split"

for name, ps in [("train", train_pairs), ("dev", dev_pairs), ("validation", val_pairs)]:
    c = Counter(p["label"] for p in ps)
    print(f"  {name:12s} pairs {len(ps):5d}  claims {len({p['claim_id'] for p in ps}):4d}  "
          + "  ".join(f"{k} {c.get(k,0):4d}" for k in LABELS))

print("\n  OK: no claim_id appears in both train and dev")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 4. tokenize
md(r"""
## 4 · Tokenize

**Premise = evidence, hypothesis = claim.** One helper, used by training and by
every evaluation below, so the order cannot drift between them.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
import torch
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
print("tokenizer:", type(tokenizer).__name__)

def encode_pair(pair):
    """(premise, hypothesis) = (evidence sentence, claim under test)."""
    return pair["evidence"], pair["claim"]

class PairDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, pairs, tokenizer, max_length=MAX_LENGTH):
        premises   = [encode_pair(p)[0] for p in pairs]
        hypotheses = [encode_pair(p)[1] for p in pairs]
        self.enc = tokenizer(premises, hypotheses, truncation=True,
                             max_length=max_length, padding=False)
        self.labels = [LABEL2ID[p["label"]] for p in pairs]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.labels)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        item = {k: v[i] for k, v in self.enc.items()}
        item["labels"] = self.labels[i]
        return item

train_ds = PairDataset(train_pairs, tokenizer)
dev_ds   = PairDataset(dev_pairs,   tokenizer)
val_ds   = PairDataset(val_pairs,   tokenizer)

lens = [len(x) for x in train_ds.enc["input_ids"]]
print(f"train {len(train_ds)}  dev {len(dev_ds)}  validation {len(val_ds)}")
print(f"token length: mean {sum(lens)/len(lens):.0f}  max {max(lens)}  "
      f"truncated at {MAX_LENGTH}: {sum(1 for l in lens if l >= MAX_LENGTH)}")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 5. warm start
md(r"""
## 5 · Warm start — permute the head, do not reinitialise it

`cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-*` already has a trained 3-way NLI head, but in
the order `{0: contradiction, 1: entailment, 2: neutral}`. Ours is
`(SUPPORT, CONTRADICT, NEI)` = `(entailment, contradiction, neutral)`.

Loading with `ignore_mismatched_sizes` or a fresh head throws away a head that
already solves 2/3 of this problem. **Permuting rows `[1, 0, 2]` keeps it.**
The permutation is derived from the checkpoint's own `config.id2label` and
asserted, never hard-coded.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoConfig

NLI_TO_VERDICT = {"entailment": "SUPPORT",
                  "contradiction": "CONTRADICT",
                  "neutral": "NEI"}

def label_permutation(id2label):
    """Column indices reordering a checkpoint's logits into LABELS order."""
    normalised = {}
    for idx, raw in id2label.items():
        name = str(raw).strip()
        verdict = name.upper() if name.upper() in LABEL2ID else NLI_TO_VERDICT.get(name.lower())
        if verdict is None:
            raise ValueError(f"cannot map checkpoint label {raw!r} onto {LABELS}")
        normalised[verdict] = int(idx)
    missing = [l for l in LABELS if l not in normalised]
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"checkpoint head missing {missing}; id2label={id2label}")
    return [normalised[l] for l in LABELS]

stock_config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
PERM = label_permutation(stock_config.id2label)
print("stock id2label :", stock_config.id2label)
print("permutation    :", PERM, "->", LABELS)

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    BASE_MODEL, num_labels=3, id2label=ID2LABEL, label2id=LABEL2ID)

with torch.no_grad():
    w, b = model.classifier.weight.data, model.classifier.bias.data
    model.classifier.weight.data = w[PERM].clone()
    model.classifier.bias.data   = b[PERM].clone()

print("head permuted into", LABELS, "order")
print("params:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) / 1e6, "M")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 6. metrics
md(r"""
## 6 · Metrics

Hand-written rather than pulled from sklearn so the zero-division convention is
explicit: a class the model never predicts scores precision **0**, not NaN. This
mirrors `researchgpt.verify.evaluate.score` exactly.
""")

code(r"""
import numpy as np

def score(y_true, y_pred):
    n = len(LABELS)
    confusion = [[0]*n for _ in range(n)]
    for t, p in zip(y_true, y_pred):
        confusion[int(t)][int(p)] += 1
    per_class, f1s = {}, []
    for i, label in enumerate(LABELS):
        tp = confusion[i][i]
        fp = sum(confusion[j][i] for j in range(n)) - tp
        fn = sum(confusion[i]) - tp
        prec = tp/(tp+fp) if (tp+fp) else 0.0
        rec  = tp/(tp+fn) if (tp+fn) else 0.0
        f1   = 2*prec*rec/(prec+rec) if (prec+rec) else 0.0
        per_class[label] = {"precision": prec, "recall": rec, "f1": f1,
                            "support": sum(confusion[i])}
        f1s.append(f1)
    return {"per_class": per_class, "macro_f1": sum(f1s)/n,
            "accuracy": sum(confusion[i][i] for i in range(n))/max(len(y_true), 1),
            "confusion": confusion, "n": len(y_true)}

def report(name, r):
    print(f"{name}   n={r['n']}  accuracy={r['accuracy']:.3f}  macro-F1={r['macro_f1']:.3f}")
    print(f"  {'class':12s} {'P':>7s} {'R':>7s} {'F1':>7s} {'support':>8s}")
    for label, m in r["per_class"].items():
        print(f"  {label:12s} {m['precision']:7.3f} {m['recall']:7.3f} "
              f"{m['f1']:7.3f} {m['support']:8d}")
    print(f"  confusion (rows=true {list(LABELS)}, cols=pred):")
    for i, row in enumerate(r["confusion"]):
        print(f"    {LABELS[i]:12s} {row}")

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    preds = np.asarray(logits).argmax(-1)
    r = score(list(labels), list(preds))
    out = {"accuracy": r["accuracy"], "macro_f1": r["macro_f1"]}
    for label, m in r["per_class"].items():
        out[f"f1_{label}"] = m["f1"]
    return out
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 7. stock baseline
md(r"""
## 7 · Stock baseline — **before** training

Scored here, on the untouched `validation` split, through the same permutation.
This is the `stock` row of the T-305 table. Taking it now means the comparison
is against the identical data and identical code path as the tuned arm.
""")

code(r"""
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
from transformers import DataCollatorWithPadding

collator = DataCollatorWithPadding(tokenizer)
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

@torch.no_grad()
def predict(m, dataset, permutation=None, batch_size=64):
    m.eval().to(device)
    loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=batch_size, collate_fn=collator)
    preds = []
    for batch in loader:
        batch = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in batch.items()}
        batch.pop("labels", None)
        logits = m(**batch).logits
        if permutation is not None:
            logits = logits[:, permutation]
        preds.extend(logits.argmax(-1).cpu().tolist())
    return preds

stock_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
y_true = [LABEL2ID[p["label"]] for p in val_pairs]
stock_result = score(y_true, predict(stock_model, val_ds, permutation=PERM))
report("stock (zero-shot)", stock_result)

del stock_model
if torch.cuda.is_available():
    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 8. train
md(r"""
## 8 · Train

Cross-entropy, fixed seed, `macro_f1` on the claim-grouped **dev** split chooses
the best checkpoint. The held-out `validation` split is not looked at until
section 9 — it is the number that gets reported, so it must not steer training.
""")

code(r"""
from transformers import Trainer, TrainingArguments, set_seed

set_seed(SEED)

args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="/kaggle/working/checkpoints",
    seed=SEED,
    data_seed=SEED,
    num_train_epochs=EPOCHS,
    learning_rate=LEARNING_RATE,
    per_device_train_batch_size=BATCH_SIZE,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=64,
    warmup_ratio=0.1,
    weight_decay=0.01,
    logging_steps=25,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    save_total_limit=1,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="macro_f1",
    greater_is_better=True,
    fp16=torch.cuda.is_available(),
    report_to=[],
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=train_ds,
    eval_dataset=dev_ds,
    data_collator=collator,
    compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
)

train_result = trainer.train()
print("\ntrain runtime: %.1f s" % train_result.metrics["train_runtime"])
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 9. evaluate
md(r"""
## 9 · T-305 — stock vs fine-tuned on the held-out set

The first time `validation` is used for anything.
""")

code(r"""
tuned_result = score(y_true, predict(trainer.model, val_ds))
report("fine-tuned", tuned_result)

print("\n" + "="*72)
print("T-305 - STOCK vs FINE-TUNED (same held-out set, n=%d)" % tuned_result["n"])
print("="*72)
hdr = f"  {'arm':14s} {'acc':>7s} {'macro-F1':>9s} " + " ".join(f"{l[:9]+' F1':>13s}" for l in LABELS)
print(hdr)
for name, r in (("stock", stock_result), ("fine-tuned", tuned_result)):
    row = f"  {name:14s} {r['accuracy']:7.3f} {r['macro_f1']:9.3f} "
    row += " ".join(f"{r['per_class'][l]['f1']:13.3f}" for l in LABELS)
    print(row)
print(f"  {'delta':14s} {tuned_result['accuracy']-stock_result['accuracy']:+7.3f} "
      f"{tuned_result['macro_f1']-stock_result['macro_f1']:+9.3f}")
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 10. gate
md(r"""
## 10 · T-307 escalation gate

Threshold fixed at **0.75 macro-F1** in `decisions.txt` D-09, *before* this run.
It is applied mechanically so the decision cannot be rationalised after seeing
the number.
""")

code(r"""
macro_f1 = tuned_result["macro_f1"]
escalate = macro_f1 < ESCALATION_THRESHOLD

print("="*72)
if escalate:
    print(f"T-307 GATE: ESCALATE.  macro-F1 {macro_f1:.3f} < {ESCALATION_THRESHOLD}")
    print("  -> set BASE_MODEL = 'cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base' in section 1")
    print("     and re-run this notebook top to bottom.")
    print("  -> latency is not a constraint (TASKLIST 0.2); cost is Kaggle time only.")
else:
    print(f"T-307 GATE: PASS.  macro-F1 {macro_f1:.3f} >= {ESCALATION_THRESHOLD}")
    print("  -> keep deberta-v3-small.")
    print("  -> spend the remaining Kaggle quota on T-332 (reranker fine-tune).")
print("="*72)
""")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- 11. save
md(r"""
## 11 · Save the checkpoint and metrics

Writes to `/kaggle/working/`, which is what the **Output** tab exposes for
download. Grab **both**: the checkpoint feeds T-304 (ONNX int8 export) and the
metrics JSON feeds T-305's table in the report.
""")

code(r"""
import os, shutil, json

trainer.save_model(OUTPUT_DIR)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(OUTPUT_DIR)

metrics = {
    "task": "T-302/T-303",
    "base_model": BASE_MODEL,
    "seed": SEED,
    "epochs": EPOCHS,
    "learning_rate": LEARNING_RATE,
    "batch_size": BATCH_SIZE,
    "max_length": MAX_LENGTH,
    "nei_per_claim": NEI_PER_CLAIM,
    "labels": list(LABELS),
    "counts": {"train": len(train_pairs), "dev": len(dev_pairs),
               "validation": len(val_pairs)},
    "stock": stock_result,
    "tuned": tuned_result,

"""T-304 — export the trained verifier to ONNX + int8, and prove it still works.

The pipeline runs on CPU with no torch at inference time (``pyproject.toml``'s
``verify`` extra deliberately omits torch), so the Kaggle checkpoint has to
become an ONNX graph before ``agents/verifier.py`` can use it.

**The acceptance criterion is a parity check, not a successful export.** An
export that silently produces garbage still "succeeds". So this runs the same
20 held-out pairs through three paths and compares logits:

``PyTorch  ->  ONNX fp32``   expected to agree to ~1e-4. A failure here means
                             the *export* is broken (wrong inputs, bad opset).
``PyTorch  ->  ONNX int8``   expected to disagree by a visible margin — int8 is
                             lossy by construction. What must hold is that the
                             **argmax still agrees**, because that is the only
                             thing the pipeline reads.

Separating the two matters: collapsing them into one loose tolerance would let
a genuinely broken export hide behind "well, int8 is lossy".

Run::

    # after downloading and unzipping the Kaggle output
    python -m researchgpt.verify.export_onnx --checkpoint data/models/verifier-scifact

    # dry-run the whole path against the stock checkpoint, before Kaggle returns
    python -m researchgpt.verify.export_onnx --checkpoint cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import shutil
from typing import Any

from researchgpt.verify.evaluate import encode_pair
from researchgpt.verify.labels import LABELS
from researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs import read_jsonl

DEFAULT_PAIRS = pathlib.Path("data/scifact/pairs_validation.jsonl")
DEFAULT_OUT = pathlib.Path("data/models/verifier-onnx")

#: ONNX fp32 must be a faithful re-encoding of the PyTorch graph.
FP32_TOLERANCE = 1e-3
#: int8 is lossy on purpose; this only catches a catastrophically bad calibration.
INT8_TOLERANCE = 2.0


def _tokenize(tokenizer: Any, pairs: list[dict[str, Any]], max_length: int, framework: str):
    return tokenizer(
        [encode_pair(p)[0] for p in pairs],
        [encode_pair(p)[1] for p in pairs],
        padding=True,
        truncation=True,
        max_length=max_length,
        return_tensors=framework,
    )


def export(
    checkpoint: str,
    out_dir: pathlib.Path,
    *,
    pairs: list[dict[str, Any]],
    max_length: int = 256,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Export, quantize, and parity-check. Returns the report dict."""
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification, ORTQuantizer
    from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig
    from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fp32_dir = out_dir / "fp32"
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)

    print(f"[1/4] exporting {checkpoint} -> ONNX fp32")
    ort_model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint, export=True)
    ort_model.save_pretrained(fp32_dir)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(fp32_dir)

    print("[2/4] dynamic int8 quantization")
    quantizer = ORTQuantizer.from_pretrained(fp32_dir)
    # avx512_vnni=False keeps the graph runnable on any x86 CPU, including the
    # examiner's laptop. The VNNI variant is faster but silently unsupported on
    # older cores, and a demo that will not start is worse than one that is slow.
    qconfig = AutoQuantizationConfig.avx2(is_static=False, per_channel=False)
    quantizer.quantize(save_dir=out_dir, quantization_config=qconfig)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(out_dir)

    int8_path = next(out_dir.glob("*quantized*.onnx"), None) or next(out_dir.glob("*.onnx"))
    print(f"      int8 graph: {int8_path.name}")

    print(f"[3/4] parity check on {len(pairs)} held-out pairs")
    torch_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint).eval()
    enc_pt = _tokenize(tokenizer, pairs, max_length, "pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits_torch = torch_model(**enc_pt).logits.numpy()

    enc_np = _tokenize(tokenizer, pairs, max_length, "np")

    import onnxruntime as ort

    def run(path: pathlib.Path) -> Any:
        session = ort.InferenceSession(str(path), providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
        names = {i.name for i in session.get_inputs()}
        feeds = {k: v.astype(np.int64) for k, v in enc_np.items() if k in names}
        return session.run(None, feeds)[0]

    fp32_path = next(fp32_dir.glob("*.onnx"))
    logits_fp32 = run(fp32_path)
    logits_int8 = run(int8_path)

    def compare(name: str, other: Any, tolerance: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
        delta = float(np.abs(logits_torch - other).max())
        agree = int((logits_torch.argmax(-1) == other.argmax(-1)).sum())
        ok = delta <= tolerance and agree == len(pairs)
        print(
            f"      {name:10s} max|dlogit| {delta:.6f} (tol {tolerance})  "
            f"argmax agrees {agree}/{len(pairs)}  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}"
        )
        return {"max_abs_logit_delta": delta, "argmax_agreement": agree,
                "n": len(pairs), "tolerance": tolerance, "pass": ok}

    report = {
        "task": "T-304",
        "checkpoint": checkpoint,
        "labels": list(LABELS),
        "onnx_fp32": compare("ONNX fp32", logits_fp32, FP32_TOLERANCE),
        "onnx_int8": compare("ONNX int8", logits_int8, INT8_TOLERANCE),
        "int8_model": str(int8_path),
        "sizes_mb": {
            "onnx_fp32": round(fp32_path.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2),
            "onnx_int8": round(int8_path.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2),
        },
    }
    print(
        f"[4/4] size: fp32 {report['sizes_mb']['onnx_fp32']} MB "
        f"-> int8 {report['sizes_mb']['onnx_int8']} MB"
    )
    return report


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="T-304 - ONNX + int8 export with parity check.")
    ap.add_argument("--checkpoint", required=True,
                    help="the unzipped Kaggle output dir, or any HF model id for a dry run")
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_OUT)
    ap.add_argument("--pairs", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_PAIRS)
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=20, help="held-out pairs for the parity check")
    ap.add_argument("--max-length", type=int, default=256)
    ap.add_argument("--keep-fp32", action="store_true",
                    help="keep the intermediate fp32 graph (roughly 4x the int8 size)")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    pairs = read_jsonl(args.pairs)[: args.n]
    print(f"T-304 - ONNX export\n  checkpoint: {args.checkpoint}\n  out: {args.out}\n")

    report = export(args.checkpoint, args.out, pairs=pairs, max_length=args.max_length)

    if not args.keep_fp32:
        shutil.rmtree(args.out / "fp32", ignore_errors=True)
        print("      removed the intermediate fp32 graph (--keep-fp32 to retain)")

    report_path = args.out / "export_report.json"
    report_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\nwrote {report_path}")

    if not (report["onnx_fp32"]["pass"] and report["onnx_int8"]["pass"]):
        raise SystemExit("T-304 FAILED the parity check - do not ship this export.")
    print("T-304 PASS: the ONNX int8 model reproduces PyTorch decisions on all "
          f"{args.n} held-out pairs.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

    ap.add_argument("--pairs", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_PAIRS)
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=20, help="held-out pairs for the parity check")
    ap.add_argument("--max-length", type=int, default=256)

``PyTorch -> ONNX fp32``  logits must agree to ~1e-3 **and** argmax 100%.

                          not on per-pair argmax.

that was the wrong test.** Measured on the stock checkpoint, dynamic int8 flips
**2 of 20** individual decisions and moves single logits by up to 4.2 — which
looks alarming — yet over the full 628-pair set it costs *nothing*:

    ONNX fp32               accuracy 0.553   macro-F1 0.516
    int8 per_channel=False  accuracy 0.554   macro-F1 0.538
    int8 per_channel=True   accuracy 0.556   macro-F1 0.539

The flips go both ways and cancel. A 20-sample argmax gate would have rejected
a quantization that is demonstrably free, so the gate now measures the thing
that actually matters. DeBERTa's disentangled attention is genuinely
quantization-sensitive per-logit; it just does not matter in aggregate.

``per_channel=True`` is the default on that evidence — same size, marginally
better, no downside found.

toolUseResult.originalFile:
"""T-304 — export the trained verifier to ONNX + int8, and prove it still works.

The pipeline runs on CPU with no torch at inference time (``pyproject.toml``'s
``verify`` extra deliberately omits torch), so the Kaggle checkpoint has to
become an ONNX graph before ``agents/verifier.py`` can use it.

**The acceptance criterion is a parity check, not a successful export.** An
export that silently produces garbage still "succeeds". So this runs the same
20 held-out pairs through three paths and compares logits:

``PyTorch  ->  ONNX fp32``   expected to agree to ~1e-4. A failure here means
                             the *export* is broken (wrong inputs, bad opset).
``PyTorch  ->  ONNX int8``   expected to disagree by a visible margin — int8 is
                             lossy by construction. What must hold is that the
                             **argmax still agrees**, because that is the only
                             thing the pipeline reads.

Separating the two matters: collapsing them into one loose tolerance would let
a genuinely broken export hide behind "well, int8 is lossy".

Run::

    # after downloading and unzipping the Kaggle output
    python -m researchgpt.verify.export_onnx --checkpoint data/models/verifier-scifact

    # dry-run the whole path against the stock checkpoint, before Kaggle returns
    python -m researchgpt.verify.export_onnx --checkpoint cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-small
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import pathlib
import shutil
from typing import Any

from researchgpt.verify.evaluate import encode_pair
from researchgpt.verify.labels import LABELS
from researchgpt.verify.scifact_pairs import read_jsonl

DEFAULT_PAIRS = pathlib.Path("data/scifact/pairs_validation.jsonl")
DEFAULT_OUT = pathlib.Path("data/models/verifier-onnx")

#: ONNX fp32 must be a faithful re-encoding of the PyTorch graph.
FP32_TOLERANCE = 1e-3
#: int8 is lossy on purpose; this only catches a catastrophically bad calibration.
INT8_TOLERANCE = 2.0


def _tokenize(tokenizer: Any, pairs: list[dict[str, Any]], max_length: int, framework: str):
    return tokenizer(
        [encode_pair(p)[0] for p in pairs],
        [encode_pair(p)[1] for p in pairs],
        padding=True,
        truncation=True,
        max_length=max_length,
        return_tensors=framework,
    )


def export(
    checkpoint: str,
    out_dir: pathlib.Path,
    *,
    pairs: list[dict[str, Any]],
    max_length: int = 256,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Export, quantize, and parity-check. Returns the report dict."""
    import numpy as np
    import torch
    from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification, ORTQuantizer
    from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig
    from transformers import AutoModelForSequenceClassification, AutoTokenizer

    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    fp32_dir = out_dir / "fp32"
    tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(checkpoint)

    print(f"[1/4] exporting {checkpoint} -> ONNX fp32")
    ort_model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint, export=True)
    ort_model.save_pretrained(fp32_dir)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(fp32_dir)

    print("[2/4] dynamic int8 quantization")
    quantizer = ORTQuantizer.from_pretrained(fp32_dir)
    # avx512_vnni=False keeps the graph runnable on any x86 CPU, including the
    # examiner's laptop. The VNNI variant is faster but silently unsupported on
    # older cores, and a demo that will not start is worse than one that is slow.
    qconfig = AutoQuantizationConfig.avx2(is_static=False, per_channel=False)
    quantizer.quantize(save_dir=out_dir, quantization_config=qconfig)
    tokenizer.save_pretrained(out_dir)

    int8_path = next(out_dir.glob("*quantized*.onnx"), None) or next(out_dir.glob("*.onnx"))
    print(f"      int8 graph: {int8_path.name}")

    print(f"[3/4] parity check on {len(pairs)} held-out pairs")
    torch_model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(checkpoint).eval()
    enc_pt = _tokenize(tokenizer, pairs, max_length, "pt")
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits_torch = torch_model(**enc_pt).logits.numpy()

    enc_np = _tokenize(tokenizer, pairs, max_length, "np")

    import onnxruntime as ort

    def run(path: pathlib.Path) -> Any:
        session = ort.InferenceSession(str(path), providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
        names = {i.name for i in session.get_inputs()}
        feeds = {k: v.astype(np.int64) for k, v in enc_np.items() if k in names}
        return session.run(None, feeds)[0]

    fp32_path = next(fp32_dir.glob("*.onnx"))
    logits_fp32 = run(fp32_path)
    logits_int8 = run(int8_path)

    def compare(name: str, other: Any, tolerance: float) -> dict[str, Any]:
        delta = float(np.abs(logits_torch - other).max())
        agree = int((logits_torch.argmax(-1) == other.argmax(-1)).sum())
        ok = delta <= tolerance and agree == len(pairs)
        print(
            f"      {name:10s} max|dlogit| {delta:.6f} (tol {tolerance})  "
            f"argmax agrees {agree}/{len(pairs)}  {'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}"
        )
        return {"max_abs_logit_delta": delta, "argmax_agreement": agree,
                "n": len(pairs), "tolerance": tolerance, "pass": ok}

    report = {
        "task": "T-304",
        "checkpoint": checkpoint,
        "labels": list(LABELS),
        "onnx_fp32": compare("ONNX fp32", logits_fp32, FP32_TOLERANCE),
        "onnx_int8": compare("ONNX int8", logits_int8, INT8_TOLERANCE),
        "int8_model": str(int8_path),
        "sizes_mb": {
            "onnx_fp32": round(fp32_path.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2),
            "onnx_int8": round(int8_path.stat().st_size / 1e6, 2),
        },
    }
    print(
        f"[4/4] size: fp32 {report['sizes_mb']['onnx_fp32']} MB "
        f"-> int8 {report['sizes_mb']['onnx_int8']} MB"
    )
    return report


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="T-304 - ONNX + int8 export with parity check.")
    ap.add_argument("--checkpoint", required=True,
                    help="the unzipped Kaggle output dir, or any HF model id for a dry run")
    ap.add_argument("--out", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_OUT)
    ap.add_argument("--pairs", type=pathlib.Path, default=DEFAULT_PAIRS)
    ap.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=20, help="held-out pairs for the parity check")
    ap.add_argument("--max-length", type=int, default=256)
    ap.add_argument("--keep-fp32", action="store_true",
                    help="keep the intermediate fp32 graph (roughly 4x the int8 size)")
    args = ap.parse_args(argv)

    pairs = read_jsonl(args.pairs)[: args.n]
    print(f"T-304 - ONNX export\n  checkpoint: {args.checkpoint}\n  out: {args.out}\n")

    report = export(args.checkpoint, args.out, pairs=pairs, max_length=args.max_length)

    if not args.keep_fp32:
        shutil.rmtree(args.out / "fp32", ignore_errors=True)
        print("      removed the intermediate fp32 graph (--keep-fp32 to retain)")

    report_path = args.out / "export_report.json"
    report_path.write_text(json.dumps(report, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
    print(f"\nwrote {report_path}")

    if not (report["onnx_fp32"]["pass"] and report["onnx_int8"]["pass"]):
        raise SystemExit("T-304 FAILED the parity check - do not ship this export.")
